text: Mars. Minus sixty degrees. Air pressure less than one percent of Earth's. Lose this helmet... and you'd have about fifteen seconds.
Okay... Mars is officially trying to kill us.
What if LEGO humans... had to live on Mars?
Welcome back to the Brick Lab! Today's question is red, freezing, and very, very far away.
Mars! Easy. Fly there, plant a flag, build a house!
Max... Mars is, on average, two hundred twenty-five million kilometers away.
And we can't just launch whenever we like. Earth and Mars line up for the best trip only once every twenty-six months.
So... let's skip the paperwork!
Yes!
Did it just build our spacesuits?
Even with good timing, the trip takes about seven months. NASA's Perseverance rover spent two hundred and three days getting there.
Professor, why do we sleep next to the water tanks?
Radiation! Water is great shielding. Out here we soak up a couple hundred times Earth's dose.
Mars: about half Earth's width, with a volcano two and a half times taller than Everest, and a canyon nearly as long as the United States is wide.
Landing is brutal. You hit the atmosphere at nearly twenty thousand kilometers per hour... and have about seven minutes to stop.
A heavy human lander needs rockets firing all the way down. The air's too thin for parachutes alone.
We're... down?
The sky... it's butterscotch.
Fine dust hangs in the thin air, turning the daytime sky a hazy caramel.
Whoa! I'm a superhero!
Mars gravity is just thirty-eight percent of Earth's. You feel lighter, but your mass is the same. Stopping is just as hard!
Ninety-five percent carbon dioxide. Almost no oxygen.
And pressure so low, the water in your body would boil at body temperature. These suits never come off outside.
The average temperature on Mars is about minus sixty Celsius. A summer noon at the equator can reach twenty degrees, but nights plunge below minus seventy.
Earth has a magnetic shield. Mars lost its global field billions of years ago.
So one sol here equals months of Earth's natural radiation.
Perfect garden dirt!
Perchlorates! Toxic salts!
Up to one percent of the soil. It must be washed before anything grows.
Rule one of Mars: hide from the sky. Burying habitats under a few meters of soil blocks much of the radiation.
Finally! Helmets off!
Pressurized, heated, and buried. Our own little bubble of Earth.
Perseverance's MOXIE experiment proved it. We can make oxygen straight from Mars' carbon dioxide.
For rocket fuel home, we'd need one about two hundred times bigger.
Ice! Barely a meter under the dirt!
Melt it, filter it: water. Split it with electricity: even more oxygen.
Martian potatoes!
Sunlight here is only forty-three percent of Earth's. The LEDs help.
Plus washed soil and added nitrogen.
Solar works, until dust covers it. So we'd add small fission reactors. NASA already tested one built for exactly this.
A Mars day, a sol, lasts twenty-four hours and thirty-nine minutes. A Mars year? Six hundred eighty-seven Earth days.
So I get a birthday every two years?!
Hi Mom! ... Mom?
Radio signals take between three and twenty-two minutes to reach Earth. There are no real-time calls home.
Dust storm! Some grow until they cover the whole planet. One ended the Opportunity rover's mission in 2018. Secure the panels!
Okay... Mars is officially trying to kill us.
Then let's not let it win.
Martian winds can top a hundred kilometers per hour, but the air's so thin it feels like a gentle push. The real danger? Dust blocking sunlight for weeks.
Long-term low gravity is a mystery. In orbit, astronauts lose about one percent of bone mass a month. On Mars, we exercise every single day.
What about kids born here? Could they ever visit Earth?
Honestly? Nobody knows. Their bones and hearts might never be ready for Earth's gravity.
Can't we just turn Mars into Earth?
A 2018 study found all the reachable carbon dioxide would give Mars only about two percent of Earth's air pressure.
And Martian sunsets are blue. Fine dust scatters blue light toward your eyes, right around the setting Sun.
From Mars, Earth is just a bright evening star. Everyone you've ever known, inside one tiny point of light.
Home.
So, could LEGO humans live on Mars? Yes. But underground, inside bubbles, making our own air, water, and food. Every breath, engineered.
Wait. Why is that moon rising in the west?
Phobos laps Mars three times a sol. And it's slowly falling. Someday, it'll be torn apart.
If Mars can lose its moon... what if Earth lost ours?
Ooh. Now that's a what-if.
